66cb1e68848f.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Argon globally, limited to paid Gemini plans and API
66cb1e68848f.dek: Gemini 4 Argon is available via API at $2/$10 per million tokens through November 30, and to AI Pro and Ultra subscribers; Antigravity and AI Studio access is Ultra-only, per Ars Technica.
keyPoints: Google says Argon is available via the API and to AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search. Antigravity access is Ultra-only, and Ars Technica reports AI Studio is too.
Introductory API pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input 95% off. Ars Technica reports rates double to $4/$20 after November 30.
Google says Argon ranks #1 on the Vals Index. Artificial Analysis puts it level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at about 60% of Astra's cost per task.
Google reports 35%+ more agentic code submissions and nearly one-third fewer rollbacks in Antigravity. Latent Space notes these are internal claims, not controlled productivity measurements.
Google is offering 10,000 scientists a free six-month top Antigravity tier and expanding to hundreds more Fairwind partners for cyber defense. Google DeepMind reports an 87% ERQA score for robotics.
66cb1e68848f.context: Ars Technica says Google revealed Argon a few weeks earlier and held back full release over misuse concerns. The launch follows a pattern of Google reserving compute-heavy models for higher-priced tiers; Ars notes free users were recently limited to Flash-Lite. Independent results are mixed: Arena ranks Argon High fifth on its agent leaderboard, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
66cb1e68848f.whatsNext: Watch November 30, when API pricing rises to $4 and $20 per million input and output tokens, and whether Google extends Antigravity access beyond Ultra, which it has declined to clarify.

e422d5ed3681.headline: Eight states sue OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT is unsafe for kids and misrepresented
e422d5ed3681.dek: Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana filed separate suits under consumer protection laws, seeking civil penalties and an end to what they call misleading safety claims.
keyPoints: The eight states filed separate lawsuits alleging OpenAI put profits over safety and failed to warn customers about ChatGPT's dangers, violating state consumer protection laws.
The states say OpenAI presented ChatGPT as a safe, youth-appropriate tool while it was dangerous to vulnerable users, including by encouraging delusions and offering dangerous medical advice.
They also accuse OpenAI of collecting data from minors and not doing enough to keep underage users off the chatbot.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says the company has built industry-leading age-specific protections, including parental controls and break reminders, and wants to work with states on AI policy for the whole industry.
The states want civil penalties and an order to stop misleading the public; some also seek deletion of unlawfully collected personal data.
e422d5ed3681.context: The suits cite earlier lawsuits from families of teens and adults who allege ChatGPT played a role in their loved ones' deaths. Arizona's complaint argues OpenAI has moved away from its original nonprofit, safety-first mission. The filings add state-level enforcement to growing legal pressure on chatbot makers over child safety.
